findings.summary: The caption's first sentence is an administrative series label rather than a hook, burying the actual hook in sentence two.
findings.evidence: "Part 2 of GIT UNDO: THE FIELD MANUAL. \"I lost my commits with reset --hard\" is almost always false — the commits are still sitting in your reflog."
findings.fix: Lead with the hook and move the part label to the end (or drop it, since the series title already carries it): "'I lost my commits with reset --hard' is almost always false — the commits are still sitting in your reflog. ... (Part 2 of GIT UNDO: THE FIELD MANUAL.)"
Run the fit pass — it adds material from the book without removing anything.

findings.summary: The recovery-window table claims unreachable objects are "gone" once `git gc` runs, but a default `git gc` deliberately preserves them via the reflog and prune grace periods.
findings.evidence: Table row: ["After `git gc` runs","gone"] — contradicting the row two lines above it, ["Unreachable, via reflog","~30 days"]. Git defaults (git-gc docs): gc.reflogExpire = 90 days, gc.reflogExpireUnreachable = 30 days, gc.pruneExpire = "2 weeks ago"; gc calls `prune --expire 2.weeks.ago`, and "an unreachable commit is never pruned as long as it is in a reflog."
findings.fix: Change the third row to reflect what actually destroys objects, e.g. ["After `git gc --prune=now`","gone"] or ["After reflog expiry + `git gc`","gone"], and optionally add a note that a plain `git gc` run right after a `reset --hard` does not lose your commits.

findings.summary: The part promises `fsck` as the rescue for a dropped stash but never shows the command anywhere, leaving the claim unusable.
findings.evidence: Page 1, section 5: "Stash is commits in disguise — fsck finds it after a drop" — `fsck` appears nowhere else in either page; the only recovery code shown is `git reflog` / `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}` / `git branch rescue <sha>`.
findings.fix: Add the concrete recovery line to section 11's code block: `git fsck --unreachable | grep commit` then `git stash apply <sha>`, so the section-5 guarantee has a matching example in the same part.
Run the fit pass — it adds material from the book without removing anything.

findings.summary: Both `@{u}` and `HEAD@{1}` ref shorthands are used in commands before either notation is defined in this part.
findings.evidence: Page 2 opening code block: "git reset --hard @{u}  # = remote"; section 11: "git reflog  # find the SHA first" followed by "git reset --hard HEAD@{1}  # undo". Neither `@{u}` nor the `HEAD@{n}` form is explained on page 1 or 2, and no sample reflog output is ever shown.
findings.fix: Gloss both at first use — annotate `@{u}` as "the upstream branch this one tracks" (or write `origin/main`), and in section 11 add one line of reflog output, e.g. `abc1234 HEAD@{1}: reset: moving to HEAD~3`, so `HEAD@{n}` = nth-previous position of HEAD is visible before it is used.

findings.summary: `clean -fdx` is ranked as the single most destructive command without ever stating what it deletes.
findings.evidence: Page 2, section 10: "`reset --hard`, then `clean -fdx` — worst" — the flags are never unpacked and the command appears nowhere else in the part.
findings.fix: Extend the bullet to name the blast radius and the guard, e.g. "`reset --hard`, then `clean -fdx` — also deletes untracked *and* ignored files (`.env`, build caches); dry-run with `-n` first".

findings.summary: "Reflog undoes anything that moved a ref" overstates coverage — Git only keeps reflogs for HEAD, branches, remote-tracking refs and notes, not for tags or arbitrary refs.
findings.evidence: Bullet: "Reflog undoes anything that moved a ref". By default core.logAllRefUpdates enables reflogs only for refs/heads/*, refs/remotes/*, refs/notes/* and HEAD, so e.g. `git tag -f v1 <other-sha>` leaves no reflog entry to recover the old target.
findings.fix: Narrow the claim to "Reflog undoes anything that moved HEAD or a branch" (tags and other refs get no reflog by default).

findings.summary: The recovery-window table lists two different survival periods without saying which one actually governs.
findings.evidence: Page 1, section 6 rows: ["Unreachable, via reflog","~30 days"], ["Prune grace period","2 weeks"], ["After `git gc` runs","gone"].
findings.fix: Add a one-line rule under the table — the shorter window wins once `gc` runs, so plan on ~2 weeks and recover fast; optionally name the knobs (`gc.reflogExpireUnreachable`, `gc.pruneExpire`).

findings.summary: The takeaway calls never-added working-tree changes "the only point of no return," ignoring the expiry/prune deadline the same part documents.
findings.evidence: "Everything Git tracks is recoverable except working-tree changes that were never added and never committed. That is the only point of no return." vs. page 1's own window table: "Unreachable, via reflog | ~30 days".
findings.fix: Qualify it: "...is recoverable while it is still in the reflog (~30 days for unreachable work, or until `gc --prune=now`). Working-tree changes never added and never committed have no window at all."

findings.summary: The decorative pushpin graphic anchored to the first yellow callout sits on top of the third code line, colliding with the comment text.
findings.evidence: Code line 3 of the top block reads "git reset --hard @{u}  # = remote" with the red pin head overlapping the gap between "#" and "= remote"; the same pin motif also overlaps "git branch rescue <sha>  # park it" in section 11.
findings.fix: Offset the pin anchor so it attaches to the top edge of the yellow callout box below the code block instead of sitting on the last code line, or add bottom padding to the code block so the pin lands in empty space.

findings.summary: Page 2 opens with an unheaded code block that belongs to section 9's reset depth ladder on page 1, so the examples arrive detached from the section that motivates them.
findings.evidence: Page 2's first block is a bare code block ("git reset --soft HEAD~3  # squash" … note "`--hard` destroys uncommitted work") with no preceding heading; the nearest heading is "9. Reset Depth Ladder" at the end of page 1.
findings.fix: Either move this code block onto page 1 directly under the section 9 table, or give it a heading on page 2 (e.g. "9 (cont.) Reset In Practice") so the reader knows which section it illustrates.
